ROYAL WOMEN OF THE UR III PERIOD
PART II: GEME-NINLILA

Piotr Michalowski
University Museum
University of Pennsylvania

The major source of information on the highest echelons of the Ur III
state bureaucracy are the tablets from Drehem. Although large numbers of
archival texts were found during the excavations at Ur, the royal
chancellery was never located. Thus while the texts from the capital do
provide us with important information on various aspects of the economy,
Drehem remains at present the main source of archival data on the political
structure of the Ur III state.

One of the most productive ways in which one can study the Drehem
tablets is through the comparison of personal names. The Ur III scribes
rarely wrote the patronymics of individuals, and official titles were not
always registered. Thus only through a careful comparison of the contexts
in which names occur is one able to reconstruct the names, functions, and
titles of particular individuals. The majority of names encountered in the
Drehem texts are masculine. Only rarely are women mentioned. Generally,
those women who can be identified by title were either wives of important
officials,! daughters of kings,? or royal consorts. To this last category
belong women who are described as dam or lukur of aruler.* Women who
are mentioned without title, however, are difficult to identify. Often, one
suspects that they were members of the royal family. Among these women
was one named Geme-Ninlila.

The most important reference to this woman is found ina text recording
the disbursement of animals for the libation places of Shulgi, his lukur
Shulgi-simti, and Geme-Ninlila.‘ Elsewhere I have suggested that Geme-
Ninlila was buried in the same tomb with Shulgi and Shulgi-simti because,
like the latter, she was also a lukur of the king.® Here we shall survey the
published texts which mention Geme-Ninlila as well as present for the first

The earliest record of this woman is dated to the eleventh month of the
thirty-seventh year of Shulgi’s reign.’ Together with other women,
including Nin-kala and Taddin-Eshtar, she was the recipient of various
precious metals and stones. Two important clues are included in this text.
First of all, the transaction was conducted in the palace (égal-kam).
Secondly, the two other women who are mentioned are most likely also
members of the royal family.

The next two texts mentioning Geme-Ninlila indicate that she had
considerable economic power. Thus Sigrist Andrews Universi

from the herd of that woman (sig udu geme>-¢nin-lil-[14]). A second tablet,
Sigrist Andrews University Tablets 1 431 (II/5 41) registers birds delivered
by two persons, including the wife of an official. The transaction is labeled
mu-TUM geme,-‘nin-lil-l4. There can be little doubt that this term has to be
compared with mu-TUM lugal and mu-TUM Shulgi-simti, “royal

The three texts edited above originated from three different months of
three different years. On the basis of this sample we may conclude that
during the last years of Shulgi’s reign Geme-Ninlila was entitled to a sadug
of thirty sheep a month, that is, one per day. Unfortunately, without a full-
scale study of the sadug during the Ur III period there is little that one can
say on the subject.!! It is not clear whether texts referring to sadugs are
records of goods given to, or on behalf of, the persons involved. However,
it is of importance that an identical sadug allotment was awarded to
another royal woman, the dowager queen Abi-simti. The following two
documents record sadugs of Abi-simti identical to the ones provided for
Geme-Ninlila. These two texts are structurally similar to those edited

In Legrain TRU 298 (IX/S 48) animals were disbursed to various deities
such as Enlil, Ninlil, and Nanna, as well as to Geme-Ninlila. It is noteworthy
that the function of maskim was held in this transaction by Arad-mu, who
only occurs in this role when persons of high social status are involved. This
text may be the last attested reference to Geme-Ninlila. There is a tablet
dated to the month $e-kin-KUD of 5 48 which mentions the receipt of three
oxen for Geme-Ninlila (BIN 5 20). The text was published as an Umma
document, and according to the calendar used in that city this would be the
first month of the year. If this text actually comes from Drehem then it
would have to be dated to month twelve.

Thus far we have been able to collect evidence which indicated that
Geme-Ninlila was the recipient of sadug offerings, took part in various
cultic ceremonies, and had other privileges which could only come to one
of very high rank. And although no text exists which would provide us with
her exact title, the cumulative data points to the conclusion that she was a
consort of king Shulgi, most probably a lukur. The final proof may be
elicited from a comparison of two archival texts from Drehem. Both record
the disbursement of equal numbers of animals from booty from the li-SU
during the second month of Shulgi year 47. It is most probable that this
booty came from a campaign against Kimash.'*

These texts are not identical. Nevertheless one may posit an analogy
between the roles of Ea-niga and Geme-Ninlila. From a number of sources
it is known that the former woman was a lukur of king Shulgi.’* In light of
the evidence gathered in this paper we may reasonably state that Geme-
Ninlila was also a lukur, and this fact would help to explain why she was
buried in the royal tomb at Ur together with Shulgi and Shulgi-simti.
